A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same coarsening-based GNN research. All pages are readable, including v2's Appendices A-D, and content can be matched across renaming, reorganization, and table changes.

before.justification: V1 reports original node and graph classification/regression results and measured inference times in Tables 7-14.

after.justification: V2 reports original predictive results, inference timings, memory measurements, and component comparisons in the main text and Appendix D.

M1.justification: Graph coarsening, Extra Nodes and Cluster Nodes augmentation, masked GCN training, and graph-level pooling retain their procedures and objectives. Explicit GCN updates and MaxPooling specify earlier pseudocode more fully; the additional named experimental configuration uses the already defined coarsened-graph model.

E1.justification: V2 adds node classification on a 165,000-node OGBN-Products community subset, extending coverage to a larger product network. All earlier datasets and the four classification/regression task families remain.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's use of Variation Neighborhoods, v2 Tables 8-9 systematically evaluate algebraic JC, kron, heavy edge, variation edges, and variation cliques across four task/dataset combinations. The Huang et al. (2021) columns in v2 Tables 4-5 identify retained baseline comparisons rather than introducing a new GNN baseline.

E3.justification: The reported coarsened-graph training budget increases from 100 to 300 epochs. Several retained classification and graph-regression comparisons change their stated augmentation from Extra Nodes to Cluster Nodes. Node-regression and graph-level timing samples increase from 20 to 1000, and v2 Table 11 specifies Gc-train-to-Gc-infer. These are reported setting revisions; the PDFs do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds systematic coarsener comparisons in Tables 8-9, Extra Nodes versus Cluster Nodes ablations across coarsening ratios in Tables 18-19, and empirical memory sensitivity results in Figure 3 and Table 17. These substantially expand evidence about component choice and resource tradeoffs; v1's theoretical Cora plots are removed.

E5.justification: V1 Table 10 reports QM9 baseline standard deviations over five runs and explains their variability; v2 Table 6 removes both that uncertainty reporting and the run-count disclosure. The node-task practice of reporting the best ten results from twenty runs remains.

E6.justification: Node-regression values and trends change substantially: Chameleon's normalized MAE at r=0.7 changes from 0.040 in v1 Table 7 to 0.591 in v2 Table 20. QM9 baseline errors are also replaced. Under revised settings, graph-level timings in v2 Table 11 show near parity instead of v1 Table 14's large speedups. OGBN-Products, memory, and component-comparison results are added.

T1.justification: V2 introduces a one-layer indistinguishability lemma and proof, two-hop information-loss formulas and cluster-feature analysis in Appendix B, and sparse-graph complexity expressions. Table 2 replaces summed subgraph memory costs with a maximum. The earlier inference-time bound and proof remain as Lemma 2.

C1.justification: The central coarsening/subgraph contribution and four task families remain. V2 promotes memory savings and low-resource applicability into its main claims, emphasizing single-node inference and quantifying benefits as up to 100-fold faster inference and 70-fold lower memory consumption.

C2.justification: V1 interprets finer partitions as improving node-regression representations; v2 reverses this explanation, attributing poorer results to lost neighboring information. Graph-level timing discussion changes from large speedups to comparable performance. Appendix B adds qualifications about retained information and cluster-feature similarity, while the experiments explicitly acknowledge that memory constraints prevent evaluating full OGBN-Products.

D1.justification: V2 discloses CPU, RAM, A100 GPU, PyTorch Geometric, MaxPooling, and OGBN subset-construction details, and changes the printed code-repository pointer. Conversely, it omits v1's numerical definitions of the few and random node-classification splits. These are mixed changes in reproducibility information, not evidence of a hardware change.

R1.justification: V2 adds Hu et al. (2020) for OGBN and Traag et al. (2019) for Leiden community extraction. Its abstract softens the blanket assertion that previous research did not address inference costs. Positioning relative to the principal GNN, coarsening, and partitioning works otherwise remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and experimental discussion undergo substantial rewriting. Shared augmentation exposition precedes task-specific methodology, dataset and hyperparameter material moves into organized appendices, and FIT-GNN terminology and numbered section hierarchy are introduced throughout.

P2.justification: Tables are extensively reformatted and reorganized: graph-classification results are transposed, node timing tables are merged, and dataset summaries move to the appendix. New comparison, memory, and ablation tables are added. Figures 1-2 are redrawn, and Figure 3 replaces two theoretical Cora plots with an empirical Physics memory chart.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens empirical support through memory measurements, a larger graph benchmark, and direct component comparisons. The net gain is limited by omitted split counts and QM9 uncertainty, unexplained Chameleon discrepancies between Tables 19 and 20, and a new Lemma 1 proof that counts retained neighbors without establishing equivalence under GCN degree normalization.
